records.source: Καὶ διασωθέντες τότε ἐπέγνωμεν ὅτι Μελίτη ἡ νῆσος καλεῖται.
records.gloss: And having been saved, then we found out that Malta the island is called.
pieces: Once we were safely ashore, we found out that the island was called Malta.

L.1: And when we had been brought safely through, then we learned that the island was called Malta.

R.1: We had all come safely to land. Then we learned that the island was named Malta.

decisions.choice: we: the narrator counts himself among those on the ship
alternatives: a source the narrator is quoting
decisions.reason: The account has spoken of "we" since 27:1, and it goes on doing so until Paul reaches Rome (28:16). The narrator presents himself as one of the travelers. The text does not name him.

decisions.choice: brought safely through: rescued from the sea onto land
decisions.reason: The same verb ends the shipwreck story in 27:44: everyone was brought safely to land. It means rescue from danger here.

decisions.choice: Malta: the island south of Sicily
alternatives: Mljet, an island in the Adriatic Sea that was also called by this name
decisions.reason: The name was used for Malta and for an Adriatic island. The ship had been driven west from Crete (27:14-27), and from this island it sails on to Syracuse in Sicily (28:12), which fits Malta.

decisions.choice: safely ashore (B); had all come safely to land (R)
decisions.reason: The verb looks back on the rescue from the wreck in 27:44, so Balanced and Readable say that they had reached land.

records.heading: Paul and the viper on Malta

records.source: οἵ τε βάρβαροι παρεῖχον οὐ τὴν τυχοῦσαν φιλανθρωπίαν ἡμῖν, ἅψαντες γὰρ πυρὰν προσελάβοντο πάντας ἡμᾶς διὰ τὸν ὑετὸν τὸν ἐφεστῶτα καὶ διὰ τὸ ψῦχος.
records.gloss: The and natives were showing not the ordinary kindness to us; having kindled for a fire they received all of us because of the rain the coming on and because of the cold.
pieces: The local people treated us with remarkable kindness. Because it had started to rain and it was cold, they lit a fire and made all of us welcome.

L.2: And the natives showed us no ordinary kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold.

R.2: The people who lived on the island were very kind to us. It had begun to rain, and it was cold. So they built a fire and welcomed every one of us.

decisions.choice: the natives: the islanders, people whose language was not Greek
decisions.reason: The word was used of anyone who did not speak Greek; it named a language, not a lack of manners, as Paul's own use shows (Romans 1:14, 1 Corinthians 14:11). Malta had been settled by Phoenicians and later ruled by Carthage, and Punic inscriptions have been found there, so the islanders probably spoke a Punic dialect. The story itself shows them as generous hosts.

decisions.choice: no ordinary kindness: unusual, remarkable kindness
decisions.reason: Saying "not ordinary" is a way of saying "extraordinary". The word for kindness is the friendliness shown to strangers, as in 27:3.

decisions.choice: welcomed: took in as guests
decisions.reason: The verb means to receive someone as a guest. Here the welcome is around the fire, in the open.

decisions.choice: the local people (B); the people who lived on the island (R)
decisions.reason: The English word "barbarians" now means violent or uncivilized people, which is not what the Greek says. Literal uses "the natives"; Balanced and Readable speak of the people of the island.

records.source: συστρέψαντος δὲ τοῦ Παύλου φρυγάνων τι πλῆθος καὶ ἐπιθέντος ἐπὶ τὴν πυράν, ἔχιδνα ἀπὸ τῆς θέρμης ἐξελθοῦσα καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Having gathered now the Paul of sticks a quantity and having laid [them] on the fire, a viper out from the heat having come out fastened on the hand of him.
pieces: Paul collected an armful of sticks and laid them on the fire. The heat brought out a viper, which clamped onto his hand.

L.3: Now when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid [them] on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.

R.3: Paul picked up a pile of sticks and put them on the fire. The heat made a poisonous snake come out of the sticks, and it bit Paul's hand and held on.

decisions.choice: a viper: a poisonous snake
decisions.reason: The word names a poisonous snake, and the islanders expect Paul to swell up or drop dead (28:6).

decisions.choice: fastened on: took hold of and clung to
decisions.reason: The verb means to seize or fasten onto. In 28:4 the creature is still hanging from his hand, and the islanders expect its poison to work, so it had bitten him.

decisions.choice: because of the heat: the heat drove it out
decisions.reason: The phrase gives the cause: the viper had been among the sticks, and the warmth of the fire roused it.

decisions.choice: it bit Paul's hand and held on
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the islanders assume in 28:4-6, that the snake had bitten him.

records.source: ὡς δὲ εἶδον οἱ βάρβαροι κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ, πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἔλεγον· Πάντως φονεύς ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος ὃν διασωθέντα ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης ἡ δίκη ζῆν οὐκ εἴασεν.
records.gloss: When then saw the natives hanging the beast from the hand of him, to one another they began to say, By all means a murderer is the man this, whom having been saved from the sea the Justice to live not has permitted.
pieces: When the local people saw the creature dangling from his hand, they said to one another, "This man is surely a murderer. He came safely out of the sea, yet Justice will not let him live."

L.4: And when the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they began to say to one another, "No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has been brought safely through from the sea, Justice has not allowed to live."

R.4: The people of the island saw the snake hanging from Paul's hand. They said to each other, "This man must have killed someone! He was saved from the sea, but the goddess Justice will not let him go on living."

decisions.choice: Justice: the goddess of justice, who punishes wrongdoers
alternatives: justice as an idea, without a goddess
decisions.reason: The Greek word has the article and is personified here. Greeks spoke of Justice as a goddess who tracks down the guilty, and the islanders' own beliefs probably had a similar figure. They reason that a man who escaped the sea and was then bitten must be guilty of some crime.

decisions.choice: creature: a wild animal, here the viper
decisions.reason: The word can mean any wild animal, small or large; here it is the viper of 28:3.

decisions.choice: no doubt: they are sure of it
decisions.reason: The adverb expresses certainty: it must be so.

decisions.choice: the goddess Justice
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the goddess" so readers know that Justice is a divine figure in the islanders' belief, not the law courts.

records.source: ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀποτινάξας τὸ θηρίον εἰς τὸ πῦρ ἔπαθεν οὐδὲν κακόν·
records.gloss: The [one] indeed then having shaken off the creature into the fire suffered no injury.
pieces: But Paul shook the creature off into the fire and was not harmed at all.

L.5: He, however, shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.

R.5: But Paul shook the snake off into the fire. Nothing bad happened to him.

decisions.choice: no harm: Jesus's promise kept
decisions.reason: In Luke 10:19 Jesus tells his followers that they may tread on snakes and nothing will hurt them. Luke does not cite the saying here, so the link is only an echo.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Paul to make the contrast with the islanders clear.

records.source: οἱ δὲ προσεδόκων αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι ἢ καταπίπτειν ἄφνω νεκρόν.
records.gloss: The but they were expecting him to be about to swell up or to fall down suddenly dead.
pieces: They kept waiting for him to swell up or suddenly drop dead.

L.6: But they were expecting that he was about to swell up or suddenly fall down dead.

R.6: The people waited. They thought his body would swell up, or that he would fall down dead at any moment.

decisions.choice: swell up: become swollen from the poison
decisions.reason: The verb can mean either to swell or to be inflamed with fever. Both describe the effect of a poisonous bite; swelling is the more common sense in medical writing.

decisions.choice: they were expecting: they watched and waited
decisions.reason: The imperfect shows them waiting over some time, which 28:6 goes on to say.

records.source: ἐπὶ πολὺ δὲ αὐτῶν προσδοκώντων καὶ θεωρούντων μηδὲν ἄτοπον εἰς αὐτὸν γινόμενον, μεταβαλόμενοι ἔλεγον αὐτὸν εἶναι θεόν.
records.gloss: A while great however of them waiting and seeing nothing amiss to him happening, having changed their opinion they began declaring him to be a god.
pieces: After a long wait, when they saw that nothing strange was happening to him, they changed their view and began to say that he was a god.

L.6: But after they had waited a long while and saw nothing unusual happening to him, they changed their minds and began to say that he was a god.

R.6: They waited a long time, but nothing at all happened to him. So they changed their minds. Now they said, "He must be a god!"

decisions.choice: a god: a divine being in their beliefs
decisions.reason: The islanders move from one belief to its opposite: first a murderer punished by Justice, then a god. The crowd at Lystra did the same in reverse (14:11-19). Luke records their opinion without comment.

decisions.choice: nothing unusual: nothing out of place, no harm
decisions.reason: The word means something out of place or amiss; here it is the effect of the bite they were waiting for.

decisions.choice: direct speech: "He must be a god!"
alternatives: they began to say that he was a god
decisions.reason: Readable turns the reported speech into a short quotation; the meaning is the same.

records.source: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς περὶ τὸν τόπον ἐκεῖνον ὑπῆρχεν χωρία τῷ πρώτῳ τῆς νήσου ὀνόματι Ποπλίῳ, ὃς ἀναδεξάμενος ἡμᾶς τρεῖς ἡμέρας φιλοφρόνως ἐξένισεν.
records.gloss: In now the [parts] around the place that were lands belonging to the chief of the island, named Publius, who having received us three days hospitably entertained [us].
pieces: Near that spot there was an estate that belonged to the leading man of the island, whose name was Publius. He took us in and treated us as his guests for three days.

L.7: Now in the [area] around that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained [us] hospitably for three days.

R.7: Near there was some land owned by Publius, the most important official on the island. He welcomed us into his home, and for three days he took good care of us as his guests.

decisions.choice: the chief man of the island: the title of Malta's leading official
alternatives: simply the richest or most important man there
decisions.reason: Greek and Latin inscriptions from Malta use this same title, "first" of the Maltese, for an official. Luke gives Publius his local title, as he gives exact titles elsewhere ("city officials" at Thessalonica, 17:6).

decisions.choice: Publius: a Roman name
decisions.reason: Publius is a Roman first name, which fits a leading official on an island under Roman rule.

decisions.choice: us: Paul and his companions, perhaps not all 276 on board
decisions.reason: The text does not say whether Publius hosted everyone from the ship (27:37) or only Paul's group. In this account "we" usually means Paul and his companions.

decisions.choice: the most important official
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that this is an official title, as the meaning note explains.

records.heading: Healing on the estate of Publius

records.source: ἐγένετο δὲ τὸν πατέρα τοῦ Ποπλίου πυρετοῖς καὶ δυσεντερίῳ συνεχόμενον κατακεῖσθαι, πρὸς ὃν ὁ Παῦλος εἰσελθὼν καὶ προσευξάμενος ἐπιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῷ ἰάσατο αὐτόν.
records.gloss: It came to pass then the father of the Publius with fevers and dysentery oppressed to be lying, to whom the Paul having entered and having prayed, having laid the hands on him healed him.
pieces: The father of Publius lay ill with bouts of fever and dysentery. Paul visited him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him.

L.8: And it happened that the father of Publius was lying [sick], suffering from fevers and dysentery. Paul went in to him, and after praying [and] laying [his] hands on him, he healed him.

R.8: Publius's father was in bed. He was sick with a fever that kept coming back, and he had a bad stomach sickness. Paul went in to see him and prayed. Then Paul put his hands on him and made him well.

decisions.choice: fevers: attacks of fever that come and go
decisions.reason: The word is plural, which suits fever that returns in bouts.

decisions.choice: dysentery: a disease of the bowels with severe diarrhea
decisions.reason: The word is the regular term for dysentery in Greek medical writing.

decisions.choice: prayed and laid hands on him: the healing comes from God through prayer
decisions.reason: Paul prays first. Elsewhere in Acts healing is credited to God or to Jesus (3:12-16, 9:34, 19:11).

decisions.choice: a bad stomach sickness
decisions.reason: Readable describes the illness in plain words instead of using the medical term.

records.source: τούτου δὲ γενομένου καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ οἱ ἐν τῇ νήσῳ ἔχοντες ἀσθενείας προσήρχοντο καὶ ἐθεραπεύοντο, οἳ καὶ πολλαῖς τιμαῖς ἐτίμησαν ἡμᾶς καὶ ἀναγομένοις ἐπέθεντο τὰ πρὸς τὰς χρείας.
records.gloss: Of this then having taken place, also the rest the in the island having infirmities were coming and were healed, \v 10 who also with many honors honored us and on setting sail they put on [us] the things for the needs.
pieces: After that, the rest of the island's sick people kept coming to him, and they were healed.
They heaped honors on us, and when the time came to sail, they loaded the ship with what we needed.

L.9: And when this had happened, the rest also who had illnesses on the island were coming and being healed,
L.10: who also honored us with many honors, and when we were setting sail they put on board the things [we needed].

R.9: After that, all the other sick people on the island came to Paul, and they were made well too.
R.10: The people gave us many gifts to honor us. When it was time for us to leave on a ship, they brought on board everything we would need for the trip.

decisions.choice: kept coming and were being healed: a stream of sick people over the winter
decisions.reason: Both verbs are imperfect: people came one after another during the three months on the island (28:11).

decisions.choice: honored us with many honors: marks of respect, which may include gifts
decisions.reason: The word for honor can include gifts or payment. The next clause shows that the islanders gave them supplies, but the text does not say that anything was paid for healing.

decisions.choice: put on board: loaded onto the ship for them
decisions.reason: With sailing, the verb means to put supplies on the ship.

decisions.choice: kept coming to him (B); came to Paul (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names Paul as the one they came to, which the context implies.

decisions.choice: gave us many gifts to honor us
decisions.reason: Readable takes the honors as gifts, the most likely sense in a list with supplies; the meaning note says this is not certain.

records.source: Μετὰ δὲ τρεῖς μῆνας ἀνήχθημεν ἐν πλοίῳ παρακεχειμακότι ἐν τῇ νήσῳ Ἀλεξανδρίνῳ, παρασήμῳ Διοσκούροις.
records.gloss: After then three months we sailed in a ship having wintered in the island, Alexandrian, with a figurehead of the Dioscuri.
pieces: Three months later we set sail on a ship from Alexandria that had spent the winter at the island. Its figurehead was the Twin Brothers.

L.11: And after three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, with the Twin Brothers as [its] figurehead.

R.11: Three months later we left on another ship. It came from the city of Alexandria, and it had stayed at the island for the winter. The front of the ship had a carving of the Twin Brothers, two gods that sailors prayed to.

decisions.choice: the Twin Brothers: Castor and Pollux, gods thought to protect sailors
alternatives: a ship named after them, with no figure
decisions.reason: The Greek name means "sons of Zeus". Greeks and Romans honored these twins as protectors of seafarers. The word for the ship's sign means an emblem or figure carved or painted on the ship, which also served as its name.

decisions.choice: an Alexandrian ship: probably a grain ship from Egypt
decisions.reason: The ship of 27:6 was also from Alexandria and carried wheat (27:38). Egypt shipped grain to Rome, and ships that met the end of the sailing season wintered in harbors along the way.

decisions.choice: three months: the winter, when ships did not sail
alternatives: a stay for some other reason
decisions.reason: Sailing in winter was dangerous (27:9-12). After three months the season would have been opening again.

decisions.choice: two gods that sailors prayed to
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the Twin Brothers were so the detail makes sense.

records.heading: From Malta to Rome

records.source: καὶ καταχθέντες εἰς Συρακούσας ἐπεμείναμεν ἡμέρας τρεῖς, ὅθεν περιελόντες κατηντήσαμεν εἰς Ῥήγιον.
records.gloss: And having put in at Syracuse we stayed days three, \v 13 from where having weighed anchor we arrived at Rhegium.
pieces: We landed at Syracuse and spent three days there.
From there we weighed anchor and came to Rhegium.

L.12: And putting in at Syracuse, we stayed three days,
L.13: from where we weighed anchor [and] arrived at Rhegium.

R.12: We stopped at the city of Syracuse and stayed there for three days.
R.13: Then we sailed on and came to the town of Rhegium.

decisions.choice: Syracuse and Rhegium: a city on the east coast of Sicily and a town on the toe of Italy
decisions.reason: The route runs north from Malta to Sicily and then across to the mainland of Italy at the strait between them.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: weighed anchor
alternatives: many manuscripts read "sailed around" or "tacked about"
decisions.reason: The two Greek verbs differ by one letter. Some early manuscripts have "weighed anchor" (the SBLGNT reading), and others have "went around", which may mean the ship had to tack against the wind. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the city of Syracuse; the town of Rhegium
decisions.reason: Readable adds that these are places.

records.source: καὶ μετὰ μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγενομένου νότου δευτεραῖοι ἤλθομεν εἰς Ποτιόλους, οὗ εὑρόντες ἀδελφοὺς παρεκλήθημεν παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἐπιμεῖναι ἡμέρας ἑπτά· καὶ οὕτως εἰς τὴν Ῥώμην ἤλθαμεν.
records.gloss: And after one day having come on a south wind, on the second day we came to Puteoli, \v 14 where having found brothers we were entreated with them to remain days seven; and so to the Rome we came.
pieces: After one day a wind sprang up from the south, and on the second day we made Puteoli.
There we found some {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, who begged us to spend seven days with them. And that is how we came to Rome.

L.13: And after one day a south wind sprang up, [and] on the second day we came to Puteoli,
L.14: where we found brothers and were urged to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.

R.13: After one day the wind began to blow from the south, and the next day we came to the town of Puteoli.
R.14: There we found some {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} who believed in Jesus. They asked us to stay with them for a week. And so at last we came to Rome.

decisions.choice: Puteoli: the chief port on the Bay of Naples
decisions.reason: Puteoli was the main harbor in Italy for the grain ships from Alexandria; Seneca describes their arrival there in one of his letters. From there travelers went on to Rome by land.

decisions.choice: on the second day: the day after the wind came up
alternatives: after two full days at sea
decisions.reason: The word means "on the second day", counted from the start of the south wind; with a following wind the crossing was quick.

decisions.choice: brothers: fellow believers, men and women
decisions.reason: Luke uses the word for believers in Jesus throughout Acts (1:15, 9:30). A group of believers already lived at Puteoli, as one did at Rome (28:15; Romans 1:7).

decisions.choice: and so we came to Rome: a summary of the journey's end
alternatives: the moment of arrival in the city
decisions.reason: Luke states where the journey ends before he tells the last stage. The believers of Rome meet them on the road (28:15), and they enter the city in 28:16.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word means fellow believers, men and women.

decisions.choice: who believed in Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable explains that these were believers, not relatives.

records.source: κἀκεῖθεν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ ἀκούσαντες τὰ περὶ ἡμῶν ἦλθαν εἰς ἀπάντησιν ἡμῖν ἄχρι Ἀππίου Φόρου καὶ Τριῶν Ταβερνῶν, οὓς ἰδὼν ὁ Παῦλος εὐχαριστήσας τῷ θεῷ ἔλαβε θάρσος.
records.gloss: And from there the brothers having heard the things concerning us came out to meeting us as far as of Appius market and Three Taverns, whom having seen the Paul, having given thanks to the God took courage.
pieces: The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} there had heard about us, and they came out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of them Paul gave thanks to God and took heart.

L.15: And from there the brothers, having heard the [news] about us, came out to meet us as far as [the] Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God [and] took courage.

R.15: The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} in Rome heard that we were coming. Some of them came out along the road to meet us at the Forum of Appius, and others at Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and felt strong again.

decisions.choice: the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns: two stopping places on the Appian Way south of Rome
decisions.reason: Both were stations on the main road from the south to Rome, the Forum of Appius about forty-three Roman miles from the city and Three Taverns about thirty-three. The believers walked a long way to meet Paul.

decisions.choice: two groups of believers, who met them at two places
alternatives: one group that waited at both places
decisions.reason: The text names two places. Most naturally, some came as far as the Forum of Appius and others to Three Taverns, nearer the city.

decisions.choice: took courage: was encouraged and strengthened
decisions.reason: Paul was arriving as a prisoner. The welcome gave him new heart.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: Fellow believers, men and women.

decisions.choice: the brothers and sisters in Rome; some ... and others
decisions.reason: Readable says where the believers came from and takes the two places as two groups, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: Ὅτε δὲ εἰσήλθομεν εἰς Ῥώμην, ἐπετράπη τῷ Παύλῳ μένειν καθ’ ἑαυτὸν σὺν τῷ φυλάσσοντι αὐτὸν στρατιώτῃ.
records.gloss: When now we came into Rome, was allowed the Paul to stay by himself with the guarding him soldier.
pieces: Once we were in Rome, Paul was given permission to live in private quarters, though a soldier guarded him.

L.16: And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.

R.16: When we arrived in Rome, Paul was allowed to live in a house by himself. But a soldier was always there to guard him.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: no mention of the centurion handing over the prisoners
alternatives: many later manuscripts add that the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the camp (or the commander of the guard)
decisions.reason: Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add a sentence that the centurion handed the prisoners over, and some Western witnesses add further words. Many early manuscripts lack it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a light form of custody: living apart, under guard
decisions.reason: Roman custody could be strict or light. Paul lived in his own lodging (28:23, 28:30) but was chained to a soldier (28:20).

decisions.choice: we: the last "we" in Acts
alternatives: the narrator stays on in the account
decisions.reason: The first-person account that began in 27:1 ends here. From 28:17 the narrator tells the story in the third person.

decisions.choice: live in a house
decisions.reason: Readable draws on 28:30, where Paul lives in rented lodging.

records.source: Ἐγένετο δὲ μετὰ ἡμέρας τρεῖς συγκαλέσασθαι αὐτὸν τοὺς ὄντας τῶν Ἰουδαίων πρώτους· συνελθόντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἔλεγεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Ἐγώ, ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, οὐδὲν ἐναντίον ποιήσας τῷ λαῷ ἢ τοῖς ἔθεσι τοῖς πατρῴοις δέσμιος ἐξ Ἱεροσολύμων παρεδόθην εἰς τὰς χεῖρας τῶν Ῥωμαίων, οἵτινες ἀνακρίναντές με ἐβούλοντο ἀπολῦσαι διὰ τὸ μηδεμίαν αἰτίαν θανάτου ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἐμοί·
records.gloss: It came to pass then after days three called together he those being of the Jews leaders; having come together then of them he was saying to them, I, men brothers, nothing against having done the people or the customs the of our fathers, a prisoner from Jerusalem was delivered into the hands of the Romans, \v 18 who having examined me were wanting to release on account of the not one cause of death existing in me;
pieces: Three days later Paul called together the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, "Brothers, I have not acted against our people or against the customs of our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}. Even so, I was made a prisoner in Jerusalem and delivered into Roman hands.
The Romans questioned me and were ready to let me go, since no charge against me called for death.

L.17: And it happened after three days that he called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. And when they had come together, he said to them, "Men, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the customs of [our] fathers, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
L.18: who, when they had examined me, wanted to release [me], because there was no cause for death in me.

R.17: Three days later Paul asked the leaders of the Jews in Rome to come and meet with him. When they had come, he said to them, "Brothers, I have done nothing wrong against our people. I have not broken the customs of our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}. But in Jerusalem I was arrested, and I was given to the Romans as a prisoner.
R.18: The Romans questioned me, and they wanted to let me go. They found that I had done nothing that deserved the death penalty.

decisions.choice: the leaders of the Jews: heads of the Jewish community in Rome
decisions.reason: Rome had a large Jewish community with several synagogues. Claudius had expelled Jews from the city some years before (18:2), but many had returned.

decisions.choice: Men, brothers: a respectful address to fellow Jews, here all men
alternatives: an address to men and women
decisions.reason: The hearers are the leaders of the community, who were men, so the address needs no inclusive form. As in 2:29 and 13:26, "brothers" means fellow Jews.

decisions.choice: handed over to the Romans: Paul sums up how he came to be in Roman custody
alternatives: the Jews themselves handed him to the Romans in a formal act
decisions.reason: In 21:30-33 the Roman tribune took Paul from a crowd that was beating him. Paul speaks of the outcome: he ended up a prisoner of Rome because of the charges brought against him in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the Romans wanted to release him: the governors found no capital crime
decisions.reason: Lysias, Festus and Agrippa all found no charge deserving death (23:29, 25:25, 26:31-32).

decisions.choice: ancestors, with "fathers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: "Fathers" here means forebears; Literal keeps the Greek word.

decisions.choice: Brothers
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable drop the formal "men", as in earlier speeches to Jewish leaders, and keep "Brothers" without a setting because the hearers were men.

records.heading: Paul speaks with the Jewish leaders in Rome

records.source: ἀντιλεγόντων δὲ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἠναγκάσθην ἐπικαλέσασθαι Καίσαρα, οὐχ ὡς τοῦ ἔθνους μου ἔχων τι κατηγορεῖν.
records.gloss: Objecting however of the Jews I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, not as the nation of me having anything to accuse.
pieces: But when the Jewish leaders there objected, I had no choice but to appeal to Caesar. I did this, not because I had any charge to bring against my own people.

L.19: But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, not as though I had anything to accuse my nation of.

R.19: But the Jewish leaders there spoke against this. So I had to ask to be judged by Caesar, the emperor. I did not do this because I wanted to accuse my own people of anything.

decisions.choice: appeal to Caesar: ask for a hearing before the emperor
decisions.reason: A Roman citizen could ask that his case be heard by the emperor (25:10-12). "Caesar" is the emperor's title; at this time the emperor was Nero.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish leaders who brought the charges
decisions.reason: Paul means the leaders in Jerusalem who opposed his release (25:2-3, 25:7, 25:24). He is speaking to Jews and calls them "my nation" in the same sentence.

decisions.choice: not that I had a charge against my nation: his appeal was a defense, not an attack
alternatives: he would bring no evidence at all
decisions.reason: Paul assures his hearers that he did not come to Rome to accuse the Jewish people before Caesar.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the group Paul means, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: διὰ ταύτην οὖν τὴν αἰτίαν παρεκάλεσα ὑμᾶς ἰδεῖν καὶ προσλαλῆσαι, ἕνεκεν γὰρ τῆς ἐλπίδος τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ τὴν ἅλυσιν ταύτην περίκειμαι.
records.gloss: For this therefore the cause I called you to see and to speak with, because of for the hope of the Israel the chain this I have around.
pieces: This is the reason I invited you here, to see you and speak with you: I wear this chain for the sake of Israel's hope."

L.20: For this reason, therefore, I called for you, to see [you] and to speak [with you], for it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain."

R.20: That is why I asked you to come here. I wanted to see you and talk with you. I am wearing this chain because I believe in what Israel hopes for."

decisions.choice: the hope of Israel: God's promise to raise the dead and to send the Messiah
decisions.reason: Paul has said the same before: he is on trial for the hope promised to the ancestors, the resurrection of the dead (23:6, 24:15, 26:6-8).

decisions.choice: this chain: a real chain, binding him to his guard
alternatives: a figure of speech for imprisonment
decisions.reason: A prisoner in light custody was often chained by the wrist to the soldier guarding him (28:16). Paul may have lifted it as he spoke, as in 26:29.

decisions.choice: I called for you to see and speak with you
alternatives: I asked you to see me and to speak with me
decisions.reason: The Greek can mean that Paul invited them in order to see them, or invited them to come and see him; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: because I believe in what Israel hopes for
alternatives: because of the hope of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable says that the hope is something believed, which Paul's earlier speeches make clear (26:6-7).

records.source: οἱ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν εἶπαν· Ἡμεῖς οὔτε γράμματα περὶ σοῦ ἐδεξάμεθα ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας, οὔτε παραγενόμενός τις τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἀπήγγειλεν ἢ ἐλάλησέν τι περὶ σοῦ πονηρόν.
records.gloss: The and to him they said, We neither letters concerning you received from the Judea, nor having arrived any of the brothers reported or said anything concerning you evil.
pieces: They answered him, "No letters about you have reached us from Judea, and none of our fellow Jews who have arrived here has brought word of anything against you.

L.21: And they said to him, "We have neither received letters from Judea about you, nor has any of the brothers come and reported or spoken anything evil about you.

R.21: The leaders said to Paul, "No one in Judea has sent us any letters about you. None of our own people who have come here from there has told us anything bad about you.

decisions.choice: the brothers: fellow Jews, not believers in Jesus
decisions.reason: The speakers are Jewish leaders who have yet to hear Paul's message (28:22), so "brothers" means members of their own people, as Paul used the word in 28:17.

decisions.choice: no letters from Judea: no official word from the leaders in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Jewish communities abroad kept in touch with Jerusalem by letter and by travelers (9:2). The leaders say that no charge against Paul has reached them by either way.

decisions.choice: our fellow Jews (B); our own people (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that the word means fellow Jews here, as the meaning note explains; Literal keeps "brothers".

records.source: ἀξιοῦμεν δὲ παρὰ σοῦ ἀκοῦσαι ἃ φρονεῖς, περὶ μὲν γὰρ τῆς αἱρέσεως ταύτης γνωστὸν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ὅτι πανταχοῦ ἀντιλέγεται.
records.gloss: We deem it worthy however from you to hear what you think, concerning indeed for the sect this known to us it is that everywhere it is spoken against.
pieces: But we think it fair to hear your own views. What we do know about this sect is that it meets opposition everywhere."

L.22: But we think it right to hear from you what you think, for concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against."

R.22: But we want to hear what you believe. We know that people everywhere say bad things about this group that you belong to."

decisions.choice: sect: a party or group within Judaism
decisions.reason: The same word is used of the Sadducees and the Pharisees (5:17, 15:5, 26:5) and of the followers of Jesus (24:5, 24:14). It names a group, not, by itself, a false one.

decisions.choice: spoken against: criticized and opposed
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in 28:19 of the Jews' objections. The leaders report what they have heard, without saying what they themselves think.

decisions.choice: this group that you belong to
decisions.reason: Readable avoids "sect", which can sound like a cult, and says plainly that Paul belongs to it.

records.source: Ταξάμενοι δὲ αὐτῷ ἡμέραν ἧκον πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν ξενίαν πλείονες, οἷς ἐξετίθετο διαμαρτυρόμενος τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ πείθων τε αὐτοὺς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀπό τε τοῦ νόμου Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἀπὸ πρωῒ ἕως ἑσπέρας.
records.gloss: Having appointed then him a day came to him into the lodging more, to whom he was expounding, fully testifying the kingdom of the God, persuading then them concerning the Jesus from both the law of Moses and the Prophets, from morning until evening.
pieces: They fixed a day with him, and on it a larger group came to his lodging. From morning to evening he laid things out for them, bearing full witness to the kingdom of God and seeking to convince them about Jesus from the law of Moses and the Prophets.

L.23: And when they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at [his] lodging in greater numbers. And he explained [things] to them, bearing full witness to the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the Prophets, from morning until evening.

R.23: So they chose a day to meet with Paul. On that day even more of them came to the house where he was staying. All day long, from morning until evening, Paul talked with them. He told them about God's kingdom. He used the law of Moses and the books of the prophets to try to convince them about Jesus.

decisions.choice: bearing full witness to the kingdom of God: the message Jesus and the apostles proclaimed
decisions.reason: Acts begins and ends with the kingdom of God (1:3, 28:31). Paul speaks of God's reign, which the Scriptures promised and which comes through Jesus.

decisions.choice: the law of Moses and the Prophets: the Jewish Scriptures
alternatives: only the books of Moses and the prophetic books, not the other writings
decisions.reason: This was a common way of naming the whole Scripture. The risen Jesus explained himself from Moses and the Prophets in Luke 24:27 and 24:44.

decisions.choice: more of them: a larger group than at the first meeting
decisions.reason: The word is comparative: more came this time.

decisions.choice: trying to persuade: an attempt, with mixed results
decisions.reason: The present participle describes the effort; 28:24 tells the result.

decisions.choice: the books of the prophets
decisions.reason: Readable says that "the Prophets" means a part of the Scriptures, the books of the prophets.

records.source: καὶ οἱ μὲν ἐπείθοντο τοῖς λεγομένοις οἱ δὲ ἠπίστουν, ἀσύμφωνοι δὲ ὄντες πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀπελύοντο, εἰπόντος τοῦ Παύλου ῥῆμα ἓν ὅτι Καλῶς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐλάλησεν διὰ Ἠσαΐου τοῦ προφήτου πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ὑμῶν λέγων· Πορεύθητι πρὸς τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον καὶ εἰπόν· Ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε καὶ οὐ μὴ συνῆτε, καὶ βλέποντες βλέψετε καὶ οὐ μὴ ἴδητε·
records.gloss: And some indeed were persuaded by the things being spoken, some however were disbelieving; \v 25 discordant then being with one another they began to leave, having spoken the Paul word one, that Rightly the Spirit the Holy spoke through Isaiah the prophet to the fathers of you \v 26 saying, Go to the people this and say, In hearing you will hear and not not understand, and seeing you will see and not not perceive;
pieces: His words won some of them over, but others refused to believe.

Divided among themselves, they began to go, but first Paul said one thing more: "How right the Holy Spirit was when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spoke to your {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} through Isaiah the prophet,
saying, 'Go to this people and tell them, "You will listen and listen but never understand. You will look and look but never see.

L.24: And some were persuaded by the things that were said, but others did not believe.
L.25: And disagreeing with one another, they began to leave, after Paul had said one word: "Rightly did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
L.26: saying, 'Go to this people and say, "In hearing you will hear and never understand, and seeing you will see and never perceive.

R.24: Some of the Jews were convinced by what Paul said, but others would not believe.
R.25: They began to argue with each other, and they started to leave. But before they left, Paul said one more thing to them: "The Holy Spirit was right in what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to your {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} through the prophet Isaiah.
R.26: He said, 'Go to these people and tell them, "You will hear and hear, but you will never understand. You will look and look, but you will never see.

decisions.choice: persuaded ... did not believe: some were won over, others refused
alternatives: some agreed for a moment only
decisions.reason: The two verbs are set against each other. "Did not believe" is the opposite of believing in Jesus, so "persuaded" here means they accepted Paul's message about him.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 6:9-10, quoted from the Greek Old Testament
decisions.reason: The wording follows the Greek translation of Isaiah closely. Jesus quoted the same passage about those who heard his parables (Luke 8:10; Matthew 13:14-15), and John cites it in John 12:40.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: your fathers
decisions.reason: Early manuscripts have "your"; the later text, followed by the King James Version, has "our". Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: in hearing you will hear: you will hear over and over
decisions.reason: The doubled verb copies a Hebrew way of stressing an action. The double negative that follows is strong: they will never understand.

decisions.choice: how right ... was (B); was right (R)
decisions.reason: The adverb means that what the Spirit said was correct and fits these hearers. Balanced and Readable say it as a judgment on what the Spirit said.

decisions.choice: ancestors, with "fathers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: "Fathers" here means forebears; Literal keeps the Greek word.

decisions.choice: listen and listen ... look and look
alternatives: in hearing you will hear ... seeing you will see
decisions.reason: The repeated verbs keep the stress of the doubled verb without the Hebrew-style phrase, which Literal keeps.

records.source: ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ ἡ καρδία τοῦ λαοῦ τούτου, καὶ τοῖς ὠσὶν βαρέως ἤκουσαν, καὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῶν ἐκάμμυσαν· μήποτε ἴδωσιν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς καὶ τοῖς ὠσὶν ἀκούσωσιν καὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ συνῶσιν καὶ ἐπιστρέψωσιν, καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτούς.
records.gloss: Has grown dull for the heart of the people this, and with the ears barely they heard, and the eyes of them they closed; lest they should see with the eyes and with the ears they should hear and with the heart they should understand and should turn, and I will heal them.
pieces: For the heart of this people has grown dull. Their ears are slow to hear, and they have shut their eyes, for fear that they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them."'

L.27: For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with [their] ears they have heard with difficulty, and they have closed their eyes, lest they should see with [their] eyes and hear with [their] ears and understand with [their] heart and turn, and I would heal them."'

R.27: These people's hearts have become hard. They have stopped up their ears, and they have shut their eyes. If they did not, they might see with their eyes and hear with their ears. They might understand in their hearts and turn back to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Then I would heal them."'

decisions.choice: Isaiah 6:10 in the Greek Old Testament: the people have dulled themselves
alternatives: the Hebrew wording, where the prophet is told to make their heart dull
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew text God tells Isaiah to make the people's heart dull. The Greek translation, which Paul quotes, describes the people's own condition: their heart has grown dull and they have shut their eyes.

decisions.choice: the heart: the mind and will, where a person understands and chooses
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures the heart is where people think and decide; here it is the heart that should understand.

decisions.choice: lest ... and I would heal them: the future verb continues the purpose clause
alternatives: a separate promise that God will heal them
decisions.reason: After "lest", the Greek has a future verb, "I will heal", as the Greek Isaiah does. It belongs with "see ... hear ... understand ... turn": they closed their eyes so that none of this would happen.

decisions.choice: turn: turn back to God, repent
decisions.reason: The verb is used in Acts for turning to God (3:19, 26:18, 26:20).

decisions.choice: turn back to me
decisions.reason: Readable says who they would turn to; God is the speaker of "I would heal them".

decisions.choice: they have stopped up their ears
alternatives: with their ears they hardly hear
decisions.reason: Readable makes the dull hearing something the people do, parallel to shutting their eyes, which the Greek text implies.

records.source: γνωστὸν οὖν ἔστω ὑμῖν ὅτι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπεστάλη τοῦτο τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ· αὐτοὶ καὶ ἀκούσονται.
records.gloss: Known therefore be it to you that to the Gentiles has been sent this the salvation of the God; they also will listen.
pieces: Know this, then: this salvation from God has been sent to the Gentiles. They will listen."

L.28: Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they also will listen."

R.28: So understand this: God has sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} salvation to people who are not Jews. And they will listen!"

decisions.choice: this salvation of God: the salvation Isaiah promised all people would see
decisions.reason: Luke uses this form of the word for salvation in Luke 2:30 and 3:6, where Isaiah 40:5 is quoted: all flesh will see the salvation of God. The book ends where Simeon's song began.

decisions.choice: they also will listen: the Gentiles, in contrast to those who refused
alternatives: they will listen and obey, as a firm promise
decisions.reason: The pronoun is emphatic, and "also" may contrast them with those who would not hear in 28:24-27, or simply stress the statement: they indeed will listen.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: no verse 29
alternatives: many later manuscripts add verse 29: after he said this, the Jews left, arguing hotly among themselves
decisions.reason: The verse is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is found in later ones, followed by the King James Version, so the SBLGNT and this translation skip from verse 28 to verse 30. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Gentiles: peoples other than Israel
alternatives: only Gentiles, to the exclusion of Jews
decisions.reason: Paul has turned to the Gentiles before (13:46, 18:6) and still went on to speak to Jews. In 28:30 he welcomes everyone who comes to him.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word "Gentiles".

decisions.choice: They will listen
decisions.reason: Balanced leaves "also" unstated to keep the stress of the emphatic pronoun; the meaning note gives the two ways of reading it.

records.source: Ἐνέμεινεν δὲ διετίαν ὅλην ἐν ἰδίῳ μισθώματι, καὶ ἀπεδέχετο πάντας τοὺς εἰσπορευομένους πρὸς αὐτόν, κηρύσσων τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ διδάσκων τὰ περὶ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάσης παρρησίας ἀκωλύτως.
records.gloss: He stayed then two years whole in [his] own rented house and was welcoming all the coming in to him, \v 31 proclaiming the kingdom of the God and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, unhinderedly.
pieces: For two full years Paul lived in lodgings he rented, receiving everyone who visited him.
There he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught the things about the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, with all boldness, unhindered.

L.30: And he stayed two whole years in his own rented [lodging] and welcomed all who came in to him,
L.31: proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching the things about the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} with all boldness, unhindered.

R.30: For two whole years Paul lived in a house that he rented. He welcomed everyone who came to visit him.
R.31: He told them about God's kingdom, and he taught them about the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. He spoke boldly, and no one stopped him.

decisions.choice: his own rented lodging: a place he rented
alternatives: at his own expense, without naming a house
decisions.reason: The noun means something hired or paid for, and so a rented place, or else the cost of it: "at his own expense". With "in" and the welcome that follows, a rented place where visitors came is the more natural sense.

decisions.choice: two whole years: Paul was still waiting for his case to be heard
decisions.reason: The book does not say how the appeal to Caesar ended. Luke counts the time and stops.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God: the theme with which Acts began
decisions.reason: Jesus spoke about the kingdom of God for forty days before his ascension (1:3). The book ends where it began.

decisions.choice: boldness: openness and freedom in speaking
decisions.reason: The word is the one used of the apostles' fearless speaking in 4:13, 4:29 and 4:31.

decisions.choice: unhindered: without anyone stopping him
decisions.reason: The adverb is the last word of the book. Though a prisoner, Paul was free to preach, and nothing stopped the message from spreading.

decisions.choice: with all boldness, unhindered: kept at the end
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the Greek order so that the book ends on "unhindered"; Readable ends on the same idea.

decisions.choice: no one stopped him
decisions.reason: Readable puts the adverb as a short sentence.
